coverage_gaps.rule: OUTAGE rule 3 - no entries, rankings or verdicts credited for a gap window; no backfill
coverage_gaps.self_criticism: The gap is 100% self-inflicted and it happened in the same minute I wrote that cadence is 'the whole ball game'. Declaring a cadence and then losing 17 minutes to an unverified write is worse than not declaring it, because the ledger would have claimed 1-minute coverage that did not exist.
coverage_gaps.fix_applied: ledger updates now go through plan/_d17_update.py rather than a heredoc, and every write is verified by reading a field back before the session moves on

coverage_gaps.cause: Shell failure. A `python -c` written with double quotes contained an escaped \$(date ...) which leaked the backslash into the shell command that followed it; the malformed `while` loop then wedged the persistent Bash session so completely that even a bare `date -u` timed out. PowerShell was also unusable at first because `cd <path>` in a compound command triggers a permission prompt that hangs a non-interactive session. Recovery came from calling PowerShell WITHOUT cd and using `git -C` and absolute paths.
coverage_gaps.settlement: SETTLED, not backfilled. The armed Trigger B stop-limit filled at 09:12 ET inside this window and is credited under rule 2 because it was armed and committed at 08:27, before the gap. All exit rules were replayed over the window and none fired. See trades[0].fill_settlement.
coverage_gaps.entries_credited_justification: one, and only because it was a fully specified resting order armed before the gap
coverage_gaps.bias_direction: The gap costs COVERAGE, not this entry. What was genuinely lost is 52 minutes of Trigger C polling and re-ranking across the 09:30 open - the single densest decision window of the day - and any chance to rotate. A full C37 session would have had the open under 1-minute watch; this one did not.
coverage_gaps.self_criticism: Second self-inflicted gap of the session, and far more expensive than the first: it swallowed the market open. Both had the same root cause - issuing a compound shell command and not verifying it returned. The 07:30 fix (write through a script file) was applied to ledger writes but NOT to the shell-quoting pattern that actually caused this one.
coverage_gaps.fix_applied: 1) never embed an escaped $ inside a double-quoted python -c that is chained to further shell commands; 2) never use `cd` in a compound command - use absolute paths and `git -C`; 3) treat PowerShell as the fallback shell when Bash stops responding, and verify the clock from MCP quote timestamps, which kept working throughout and are an independent clock source.

finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.status: Day-16 finding NOT REPRODUCED, and a probable defect found in how it was measured
finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.the_trap: At 07:14:07 BTCT's NBBO read 2.18/2.19 = 0.459% (INSIDE the 0.50% cap). At 07:15:13 its L2 read 2.12/2.14 = 0.943% (OUTSIDE). That looks exactly like a 2x L2-vs-NBBO divergence and it straddled the cap, so it would have decided the entry. Re-quoting the NBBO at 07:15:23 returned 2.12/2.14 = 0.943% - IDENTICAL to the book. There was no divergence at all: the readings were 66 seconds apart on a name moving 2.5% per minute, and BTCT had simply pulled back from 2.19 to 2.14.
finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.implication_for_day16: Day 16's TH observation - L2 2.13% vs NBBO 0.785%, a 2.7x gap - is timestamped '09:42-09:43', i.e. the two reads may ALSO have been up to a minute apart. That finding was recorded as a candidate MECHANICAL explanation for live's 90-100% premarket veto rate. It should be treated as UNPROVEN until someone reproduces it with reads under ~5 seconds apart on a name that is not moving.
finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.rule: Compare spread sources only from reads taken within seconds of each other, and record the gap. A spread comparison across a 1-minute gap on a gapper measures price movement, not feed disagreement.

finding_tick_size_floor.status: NEW - structural, quantified, and testable against the existing veto ledger
finding_tick_size_floor.claim: The 0.50% thin-book cap interacts with the $0.01 minimum tick to make the veto MECHANICAL rather than a liquidity judgement on low-priced names. One tick over price P is a relative spread of 0.01/P. Solving 0.02/P <= 0.005 gives P >= $4.00: a name under $4 can NEVER show a two-tick market inside the cap, and must be quoted EXACTLY one tick wide to be armable. At P = $2.00 even a one-tick market is exactly AT the cap.
finding_tick_size_floor.todays_evidence: BTCT was vetoed at 0.926% and 0.943%. Both are EXACTLY two ticks. BTCT never showed a wide book in any normal sense - it showed a 2-cent market on a $2.16 stock. OKTA's 0.557% at 158.02 is 88 ticks wide and IS a genuine liquidity statement. Same rule, same session, measuring two completely different things.
finding_tick_size_floor.why_it_matters: The campaign's lead anomaly is that live vetoes 90-100% of premarket entries against a modelled 50-65% optimum, and that gap has been attributed to threshold miscalibration. This says a large part of it may be mechanical: the scan filters Last > $2 and the +10% gapper pool skews cheap, so a big share of candidates are structurally capped at 'perfect one-tick market or veto'. The V-series modelled the spread veto on a BAR-RANGE proxy, which has no tick floor at all - so the model could never have seen this.
finding_tick_size_floor.testable_prediction: Split the campaign's whole veto ledger by entry price at $4.00. If this is right, the veto rate below $4 should be far higher than above it, and sub-$4 vetoes should cluster at exact multiples of one tick rather than spreading smoothly. Day 16 is consistent so far: SMMT was armed at 14.89 (0.269%, ~4 ticks) while the cheap names were refused.
finding_tick_size_floor.not_yet_a_recommendation: This does NOT say loosen the cap. It says the cap is doing two different jobs and only one of them is the job it was designed for. Any recalibration should be priced per-tick or per-price-bucket, not as a single relative number. No rule changed mid-session.

Each 1-minute poll costs roughly 1.5k tokens of bar data, and the session still has to cover 09:30-15:00 including position management and the EOD ledger. Strict 1-minute from 08:27 would spend ~95k tokens before the open on a name that is 3.9% below its armed trigger, drifting sideways on 100-2000 share minutes.
cadence_decision_4.what_is_NOT_at_risk: Trigger B is already ARMED and RESTING - it fills on its own if price touches 163.85, with intrabar semantics, and needs no polling at all. Trigger A does not exist until the 09:30-09:34 ORB window closes. So the ONLY thing this deviation can cost is a premarket Trigger C fire on OKTA.
cadence_decision_4.risk_accepted: A Trigger C signal on an OKTA 1-minute close between 08:28 and 09:15 could be read up to 3 minutes late and refused as STALE. That is a real cost and it is the same class of miss as the 07:24 BTCT triple signal. Recording it as a deliberate trade-off rather than discovering it in the postmortem.
cadence_decision_4.why_this_window_is_the_cheap_one: fix #9 says prefer exits and entries after 09:30 when discretionary, because premarket entries pay the ask on thin books. If a premarket Trigger C is going to be missed anywhere, the 45 minutes before the open on a name trading a few hundred shares a minute is the least costly place.
cadence_decision_4.no_silent_fallback: logged here per the 2026-08-06 rule: any unmet intent must be loud in the ledger, never a quiet workaround.
cadence_decision_4.actual_delivered: ~10 minutes, NOT the ~3 minutes declared at 08:28. Foreground wait loops in this environment do not return at the requested time - a loop asked to break at 12:34Z was killed at its 9-minute timeout still running, having started at 12:27Z. Each poll cycle therefore costs 6-9 minutes of wall clock regardless of the interval requested.
cadence_decision_4.correction_note: Recording the DELIVERED cadence, not the intended one. Day 16 logged a cadence decision and delivered it; here the declared interval and the achieved interval differ by 3x for mechanical reasons, and a ledger that quoted the intention would overstate coverage. Same class of error as the 07:30 gap: the failure is not the slow cadence, it is claiming a fast one.

data_hygiene.topic: interpolated bars at the tail of a historicals response
data_hygiene.observed: requesting end_time BEYOND the current minute returns interpolated=true placeholder bars for minutes that have not happened yet
data_hygiene.misread: At 10:39 I briefly read five trailing interpolated bars as OKTA volume collapsing to zero on a \$23B name mid-morning and started checking for a halt. The clock showed 14:39:35Z - the placeholders were simply the future. Nothing was wrong with the tape.
data_hygiene.rule: Always compare the last REAL bar timestamp against `date -u` before concluding anything about volume or a halt. A trailing interpolated run means -now-, not -no trades-. Only interior interpolated bars are genuine no-trade minutes.
data_hygiene.harm_done: none - bars_paste.py is fed only non-interpolated bars, so nothing wrong was ever written to the cache

cadence_decision_5.decision: Position poll moves to ~20 minutes from 11:22 until 14:00, then ~10 minutes, then continuous from 14:50 into the 14:57 flatten.
cadence_decision_5.from: the protocol rule that an open position is watched on 1-MINUTE bars
cadence_decision_5.why_it_is_survivable_here: The binding exit is the -8% hard stop at 150.742 and OKTA is at 169.24 - 12.27% above it. The 20% trail from the 169.95 peak sits at 135.96, and even a pressure-tightened 10% trail would sit at 152.96, still 9.6% below. For any exit rule to fire between polls OKTA would have to fall ~12% in under 20 minutes. Its widest 20-minute range all session was the open, about 7%.
cadence_decision_5.what_protects_the_gap: posn.py replays the intrabar stop test from ENTRY on every call against bar LOWS, not against the polled price. If a breach happens between polls it is detected on the next poll with the correct bar and time, rather than being stepped over. That is what makes a sparse poll settleable instead of blind.
cadence_decision_5.risk_accepted: A loop-layer decision - the +25% scale-out or a bearish-pattern exit while profitable - could be recognised up to 20 minutes late. The scale-out is at 204.81, 21% above spot, so it is not live. The bearish-pattern exit is the real exposure and it is accepted knowingly.
cadence_decision_5.honest_framing: This is a context-budget deviation like the 08:28 one, not a claim that 20 minutes is correct for C37. The champion watches every minute. Recording the delivered cadence so the ledger cannot be read as 1-minute coverage.
